why: This file used to be a PRESERVATION manifest. Twenty-three declarations
covering thirty-three terminal writers were each answered with the same
verdict — PRESERVED_PLANNED_WRITER — which was an honest statement that the
code did not run, carried its reason, and was counted as an open wiring
backlog rather than folded into a passing total.
That was the right shape for a backlog and the wrong shape for a release.
'Preserved but wired to nothing' is not a final state: an executable writer
that nothing reaches is either a capability the product is failing to
deliver, or code that should not be in the tree. Kept indefinitely it is
the worst of both — it passes review because it is 'accounted for', it
keeps its tests green, and the first time it runs will be the day someone
finally wires it, against data nobody has re-checked since it was written.
So the file is now a DISPOSITION manifest. Every one of the original
twenty-three declarations carries a terminal disposition and the evidence
for it. PRESERVED_PLANNED_WRITER is no longer an accepted value, and the
closure gate in services/api/test/phase-13-writer-preservation-gate.test.ts
rejects it.
Three things the gate enforces, because a disposition is a claim and a
claim that cannot fail is not evidence:
- a WIRED disposition must name an integration site that exists and that
actually CALLS the writer — not merely mentions it, and not merely the
file the writer is declared in;
- a REMOVED disposition must name a file the declaration is genuinely
gone from, and the symbol must not have been quietly re-declared
anywhere else in the followable trees;
- a BACKLOG-only disposition must point at a real line in an EXISTING
architecture document. No new ledger, no new registry: if the backlog
cannot be written where the programme already keeps its backlog, it is
not a backlog, it is a second opinion.
MEASURED RESULT after this pass, from the mutation closure analyzer over
the current tree: byWriterBucket.PRESERVED_PLANNED_WRITER = 0,
byWriterBucket.DEAD_UNREACHABLE = 0, MutationWriterConservationHolds =
true, over 1209 terminal writers.
A NOTE ON THE EVIDENCE THAT USED TO BE HERE. Several v1 entries cited a
test as proof that a writer was 'driven' or 'exercised'. On inspection
most of those tests were source-text regexes over the service file, and two
were vi.mock stubs — they asserted that an identifier EXISTED, not that any
code ran. That is how a manifest starts describing itself. Where an entry
below cites a test, it cites what the test executes.

entries.capability: operator dismissal of a media-intelligence run, so a failed or superseded run stops surfacing in the reviewer console
entries.evidence: Two shipped surfaces already assumed this existed. The media-graph ops console renders a counter tile labelled 'Run dismissed (operator)' over `media_intelligence_run_dismissed_total`, a registered metric that no code path could increment, so the tile showed a structurally impossible zero. And the media-intelligence processor's own comment tells operations that a run left PENDING by an unshipped arm can be 'dismissed manually' — they could not. DISMISSED was already in the run status vocabulary with this as its only writer.
entries.integration: POST /v1/ops/media-intelligence/runs/:runId/dismiss — requireAuth + requireOpsActorAction(teamId), mirroring the sibling retry route. Takes the run ROW uuid rather than the retry route's BullMQ job id, because it acts on the row.
entries.alsoFixed: dismissRun discarded the affected count and returned ok:true for anything that did not throw, so 'run absent', 'run in another workspace' and 'already terminal' were indistinguishable from a dismissal. It now reports whether a row moved, which is what makes the route's answer and the counter true.

entries.capability: fan-out of collaboration-team notifications to the members an event concerns
entries.evidence: Two live read surfaces render CollaborationTeamNotification rows — the team collaboration console's NotificationsCard (with unread badge, mark-read and mark-all-read) and the Operations-Center unified inbox, whose route comment promises exactly this class of row. Of the ten declared CollaborationTeamNotificationType values, exactly one (MENTION_IN_COMMENT) had a producer; the other nine, ACCESS_REVIEW_OPENED among them, were dead by construction.
entries.integration: openAccessReview, inside the transaction that creates the review and its per-member items, so an access review cannot exist without the members it reviews having been told. `activeMembers` now selects userId alongside id, which costs no extra read.

entries.capability: claimed to record that a signed exchange delivery was verified by the receiving party
entries.evidence: Its docblock described 'a recipient hits the verify endpoint with a signed token'. There is no verify endpoint. The exchange lifecycle stops at DOWNLOADED — the routes are record-delivery, download, revoke, accept-transfer and complete-transfer — and the token verifier such an endpoint would need, verifySignedManifestToken in the same module, has no caller either. The v1 entry cited two tests as asserting on it; both are vi.mock stubs that return {ok:true} so an unrelated module mock is shape-complete.
entries.alsoFixed: The VERIFIED rung was removed from the delivery state ladder in listDeliveryActivity. It was derived from verifiedAtUtc, which this was the only writer of, so the operator console carried a lifecycle state no delivery could reach. PHASE_4B_PRODUCT_PACKAGING_AND_LIFECYCLE_FINAL_REPORT.md claimed 'every transition is mirrored ... via emitTransferVerificationEvent'; the transitions it names call emitTransferCustodyEvents, and that sentence has been corrected in place rather than left to be read as a description of behaviour.

entries.capability: producer for the mi-embed queue — turns newly indexed text chunks into embedding jobs
entries.evidence: Its only caller is indexEvidenceText, which was itself unwired; the two are wired or removed together, and the entry below records why the answer was wiring. The consumer side was already complete and live: a registered BullMQ worker on the mi-embed queue, a canonical registry entry with idempotency, retry and reconciler declared, a per-workspace spend gate and a workspace AI-policy gate.
entries.integration: indexEvidenceText enqueues one job per indexing pass after the chunk rows are written, policy-gated and best-effort.

entries.capability: writes the semantic chunk index for an evidence item — the whole input side of semantic search
entries.evidence: The instruction to verify no enabled UI or API route promises semantic search before removing was carried out, and it does. GET /v1/search ships a mode selector plus semanticAvailable/modeUsed/fallbackReason; GET /v1/search/semantic/status is live; POST /v1/search/semantic/backfill is live behind requirePlatformAdmin. The search page fetches that status, DEFAULTS the search mode to hybrid whenever semantic reports available, and renders a chip reading 'Hybrid semantic search active'. The admin costs page renders embedding spend tiles. Meanwhile this was the only row-creating writer of evidence_semantic_chunks in the tree and it had zero production callers, so with the flag on the product asserted active semantic search over a permanently empty index. Removing it would have orphaned ten reader sites, the whole mi-embed worker, the backfill service, two routes and the UI chip — a far larger deletion than the honest fix.
entries.integration: runExtractionInline, on the COMPLETED EvidenceExtractedText write — the moment derived OCR/transcript text first exists, alongside the two consumers already triggered there (keyword re-index, entity extraction). Gated on teamId, on SEMANTIC_SEARCH_ENABLED (chunk text is a second copy of derived content and a deployment with semantic search off should not be storing one), and inside indexEvidenceText on the workspace AI policy before anything is sent to a provider.
entries.alsoFixed: docs/architecture/phase-16-semantic-search-activation-final.md claimed the media-intelligence processor 'inherits the new behaviour automatically because it calls indexEvidenceText'. It did not call it. That row now names the real hook.

entries.capability: expires in-flight MFA recovery requests past their TTL, and requests whose email-verification link has died
entries.evidence: The v1 entry kept it on the stated ground that services/worker/src/mfa-challenge-gc.ts 'performs a DIFFERENT expiry (challenges), so this is not a duplicate authority'. Reading that file disproves it. Step 2 of runMfaChallengeGc selects status IN ('EMAIL_VERIFICATION_PENDING','PENDING_ADMIN_REVIEW') with the same expiresAt < now OR emailVerificationExpiresAt < now disjunction, then re-checks the status in the WHERE of the updateMany to EXPIRED — the same query, the same states, the same race guard. It is bounded at 200 rows a tick and armed every fifteen minutes from the worker's boot chain by startMfaChallengeGcScheduler. The expiry sweep was ARMED; this was its second copy.

entries.capability: the APPROVED -> COMPLETED transition, the only terminal state an approved recovery request can reach
entries.evidence: The schema states were read rather than assumed: MfaRecoveryRequestStatus is EMAIL_VERIFICATION_PENDING | PENDING_ADMIN_REVIEW | APPROVED | REJECTED | EXPIRED | CANCELLED | COMPLETED — there is no REQUESTED, CONSUMED or REVOKED. approveRecoveryRequest revokes every ACTIVE factor and batch-invalidates the outstanding recovery codes in one transaction, so APPROVED means 'entitled to enrol again'. Nothing spent that entitlement, so an approved request stayed APPROVED after the user had recovered, standing as a live admin-blessed permission and reported by the admin queue as still in flight.
entries.integration: verifyAndActivateEnrollment — successful re-enrolment IS the recovery-completion moment. Called after the factor transaction commits and outside it, so closing the recovery row can never roll back an enrolment whose recovery codes the user has already been shown. A no-op for an ordinary enrolment with no recovery in flight.
entries.alsoFixed: The transition was read-then-write: one findMany, one blanket updateMany, then one security event per row READ. Two concurrent completions both read the same rows and both emitted. Each row is now claimed individually with status:'APPROVED' in the WHERE and the affected count as the authority — count 1 means this caller performed the transition and may emit, count 0 means it does nothing. Exactly one effect per request under any concurrency.

entries.capability: the terminal state for an automation webhook delivery whose outcome stays UNKNOWN after reconciliation is exhausted
entries.evidence: The v1 entry said 'the reconciliation loop never calls it, so an exhausted ambiguous delivery has no terminal row'. The second clause is false. reconcileAmbiguousDeliveries writes the terminal row itself when reconciliationAttempts reaches AMBIGUITY_MAX_RECONCILIATIONS — status DEAD_LETTERED_UNKNOWN, nextAttemptAt and leaseExpiresAtUtc cleared, and the same automation_webhook_delivery_dead_lettered_unknown event — and that behaviour is covered by an executed integration test. ARCH-005 is implemented; this was its second implementation, and the weaker one: the loop writes through fencedDeliveryUpdate so its update is conditional on claimGeneration and bumps it, while this issued a plain update by id and would have dropped the fence and lost reconciliationAttempts if the loop had called it.
entries.alsoFixed: The one thing the removed helper had that the loop did not was the real runId on the emitted event; the loop emitted an empty string because it never selected the column. The loop now selects and emits it, so an operator can follow a dead-letter event back to the automation run that produced the delivery.

entries.capability: records a reviewer-ops reminder as delivered
entries.evidence: The v1 entry said no dispatcher reports delivery outcomes back to the engine. It understates it: there is no dispatcher at all. Nothing selects due reminders, nothing sends one, nothing consumes communicationMessageId, and listReminders has no route. The engine schedules — sweepDueSoonReminders and sweepInactivityReminders create rows with status SCHEDULED through scheduleReminder, genuinely driven by the cron-secret reconcile route — and the row is never touched again. DELIVERED, FAILED and SUPPRESSED are all unreachable in production. Keeping executable outcome writers made the engine look like it delivers reminders.
entries.alsoFixed: The module docblock promised 'Notification dispatch is best-effort; failure marks the row FAILED but does NOT throw', describing a delivery path that was never built. Corrected in place.

entries.capability: records a reviewer-ops reminder as failed
entries.evidence: The delivery twin of the entry above and removed with it, for the same reason: a failure outcome for a send that no code performs. Note that the metric reviewer_reminder_failed_total SURVIVES and is not residue — it counts a failed scheduling insert in the scheduleReminder catch arm, which is a thing that really happens. It never counted a failed delivery.

entries.capability: creates an enterprise organization, its first team and its owner invite in one idempotent operation
entries.evidence: The v1 entry recorded 'no platform-admin route or CLI invokes it; provisioning is performed by hand today'. That was simply false. POST /v1/admin/enterprise/provision, registered in admin-provisioning.routes.ts behind requirePlatformAdmin plus a CAPABILITY_GRANT step-up, has called it through provisionEnterpriseCustomerIdempotent since Phase 2, and the programme ledger records this as the ONLY sanctioned enterprise-org creation path. What hid it was an indirection: the wrapper read `const provision = deps.provision ?? provisionEnterpriseCustomer` and then called `provision(...)`, so the sole call expression in the file named a local variable and no static reader — the analyzer, a reviewer, or an IDE's find-usages — could see the edge.
entries.integration: provisionEnterpriseCustomerIdempotent now branches on the injected dependency instead of defaulting through it, so the production call is written out. The test seam (`deps.provision`) is unchanged and still works.

entries.capability: removes every AI record a workspace owns when the tenant is destroyed
entries.evidence: The canonical tenant destruction path was traced rather than assumed. Workspace CLOSURE (workspace-closure.service.ts) is explicitly archive-only — 'ARCHIVE access, never destroy evidence' — and the destruction orchestrator in lifecycle/destruction-governance.service.ts is EVIDENCE-scoped, taking a list of evidenceIds. The one path that physically destroys a tenant is DELETE /v1/teams/:id, which ends in prisma.team.delete. The retention question then answers itself from the schema: WorkspaceAiPolicy carries `team Team @relation(onDelete: Cascade)` and AiCopilotObservationReview cascades off its parent run, but AiCopilotRun, AiUsageEvent, AiUsageDaily, AiUsageMonthly, SemanticUsageDaily, ProviderUsageEvent and ProviderBudget each carry a BARE workspace_id/team_id uuid with no foreign key. Deleting the Team left all of them behind, naming a tenant that no longer exists, holding prompt and response artifacts and per-user attribution, unreachable by any tenant-scoped query. No retention authority requires them: the billing records this system must keep are Subscription and Payment, and the same route already refuses to run while an active subscription exists.
entries.integration: DELETE /v1/teams/:id, immediately BEFORE prisma.team.delete. The ordering is the point: a purge failure now throws with the Team — and therefore its AI rows — still present and still reachable by a retry, where purging after the delete would have converted any failure into permanent orphans.
entries.alsoFixed: Coverage was extended from four tables to seven (SemanticUsageDaily, ProviderUsageEvent, ProviderBudget were orphaned the same way), and the blanket `catch {}` was removed. A best-effort swallow on a destruction path is the worst possible shape: the purge fails, the caller deletes the Team, and nothing is reported.

entries.capability: quarantines a redaction derivative whose integrity cannot be established
entries.evidence: QUARANTINED was already read in production — requestRedactionDerivative refuses to re-render a quarantined row — and already rendered by two shipped web components whose copy names the action outright ('This redacted copy was quarantined by an administrator'). No administrator could perform it: no route existed, and `redaction.administer` was a declared capability with no leg behind it. The distinction matters beyond tidiness: the worker's failure sink writes FAILED, and FAILED is retryable (requestRedactionDerivative resets it to QUEUED on the next request), so a derivative whose integrity cannot be established would be re-rendered on a loop rather than stopped.
entries.integration: POST /v1/redaction/derivatives/:id/quarantine — requireAuth + resolveWorkspace + the existing `redaction.administer` capability gate, bounded reason. Operator-initiated by design: the function carries actorUserId, which is precisely what a worker does not have.

entries.capability: single-membership reactivation
entries.evidence: The v1 entry said 'no route offers per-member reactivation'. POST /v1/identity/members/:id/restore has offered it since Phase 17, through restoreMember in rbac.service.ts, behind the four-layer identity guard (actor membership, authorizeOrFail, managed-identity refusal, MEMBER_RESTORE step-up). That path performs the same transition — SUSPENDED to ACTIVE, suspension bookkeeping cleared, a MANUAL provenance grant recorded — and additionally emits the member audit and security event this one did not. These were not a wired leg and an unwired leg; they were two implementations of one transition, and the wired one is more complete.

entries.capability: revokes ONE grant source of a membership and downgrades the member to what the remaining sources still entitle
entries.evidence: Source-aware revocation is a real governance idea and is not a current product behaviour. No route touches membershipGrant rows at all; SCIM deprovisioning and administrative revocation both run through massRevokeWorkspaceMemberships / revokeAllMembershipGrants, which close every source at once; membership removal is deliberately all-or-nothing everywhere it is exposed. What stood here was a complete revocation path, including a legacy-provenance policy branch, that no caller had ever exercised against real data — and a revocation primitive is the worst thing to keep dormant, because the first time it runs will be during an incident, against rows whose provenance-backfill state nobody has re-checked since it was written. recordMembershipGrant, the producer, stays: grant provenance IS written today and IS read by the members projection.

entries.capability: closes abandoned upload sessions that expired without completing
entries.evidence: Its sibling in the same module, reapStaleMultipartUploads, has run on the master reconcile tick since Phase 30.8. That one releases the S3-side parts of an abandoned upload; this one closes the database-side session row. Having one of the pair armed and the other not is exactly how a session ends up with its storage released and its row still claiming INITIATED/UPLOADING/VERIFYING past its own expires_at_utc, with no terminal state, forever.
entries.integration: runMasterReconcile, behind POST /v1/ops/reconcile (INTEGRATION_CRON_SECRET), on the same tick as the multipart reaper and immediately after it — release the bytes, then close the row. Independently failure-isolated like every other step there.
entries.alsoFixed: The statement was a single unbounded UPDATE over every expired row. Every other sweep on that tick takes a bounded batch, and the first tick after an outage is exactly when the backlog is largest and a long write over a hot table least affordable. It now updates at most 200 rows per call, oldest expiry first, with the state predicate still in the WHERE so a session that completed between select and update is not clobbered.

entries.capability: repairs a workflow stage projection that has drifted from its immutable decision log
entries.evidence: WorkflowReviewDecision rows are the record of what reviewers decided; EvidenceReviewWorkflow.status is a projection of them, and a projection can drift — a crash between the decision write and the status write, a lifecycle event applied out of order. When it does, the console shows a stage the decision log does not support. Its bounded batch caller scanReviewDecisionProjections was exported and armed by nothing.
entries.integration: runReconcile, the existing bounded team-scoped idempotent sweep for this domain, already driven by the cron-secret POST /v1/reviewer-ops/reconcile route from the worker's reviewer-ops scheduler. A second scheduler sweeping the same team would have been a parallel authority for no gain. The scan's scanned/repaired counts are reported on the ReconcileResult and on the reconcile security event, so a repair is never silent.

entries.capability: recomputes the organization health projection that the command centre and the Worker's refresh job both read
entries.evidence: Originally this was the only writer of orgHealthProjection and nothing called it, so the row buildProjectionSummary reads was never written: every request took the 'missing' branch and returned two of eight counters with the rest defaulted to zero. Wiring it exposed a second defect — the arithmetic existed TWICE. The Worker's processOrgHealthRefreshJob carried its own copy WITHOUT the pipeline-status filters, so it counted a CREATED / UPLOADING / UPLOADED / FAILED_HASH_MISMATCH record as 'pending a report'. A workspace with ten stalled uploads read as ten reports outstanding from one path and zero from the other, and which number Home showed depended on whether the Worker's row or the API's live path had written last.
entries.integration: The writer now lives in @proovra/shared-runtime because the Worker cannot import from services/api, and BOTH hosts call this one implementation: command-center.service.ts refreshes on a missing or stale read, and the Worker's org-health-refresh processor delegates to it rather than recomputing. The duplicate at services/api/src/services/dashboard/projections/refresh-org-health.service.ts is deleted, so the two surfaces can no longer disagree by arithmetic — there is only one.
entries.alsoFixed: sampledAtUtc was `new Date()` while the upsert key is (teamId, sampledAtUtc), so the upsert could only ever take its create branch — an INSERT wearing an upsert's clothes, appending a row per refresh without bound. It is now floored to a one-minute bucket, so concurrent dashboard loads inside a minute converge on one row instead of racing to append.
entries.relocatedFrom: services/api/src/services/dashboard/projections/refresh-org-health.service.ts (deleted; this is a relocation of the single authority, not a removal of the capability)

entries.capability: claimed to be incident-response repair of the platform admin audit hash chain
entries.evidence: It repaired a LABEL, not a chain. For each row it recomputed the expected hash under chain version 1 and version 2 and, when one matched the stored hash, corrected the row's chainVersion column to say so; a row whose prevHash did not follow, or whose hash matched neither — an actual break — made it return early with brokenAt, repairing nothing. It was the v1-to-v2 migration's one-time backfill of chain_version. The chain is now on version 3: computeExpectedHashForRow has taken a version-3 branch since v3 shipped and verifyOrderedRows verifies against it, but this tried only 1 and 2, so run against any current database it would meet the first v3 row, match neither recomputation, and report a healthy chain as broken — an incident tool whose failure mode is to manufacture an incident.

entries.capability: deletes expired durable MFA pending challenges
entries.evidence: Described as an 'admin-callable sweep' and callable by nobody: no route, no CLI, no scheduler, and R8.1.3's own risk register records the ops endpoint that would have called it as deferred. The scheduled coverage it was waiting for had already shipped elsewhere — services/worker/src/mfa-challenge-gc.ts runs the same two-step bounded delete (consumedAt < cutoff OR expiresAt < cutoff, select ids, delete by id) on the same one-hour retention, armed every fifteen minutes. The two had already drifted: the worker drains 200 rows a tick and this drained 50, while its comment claimed the constants matched.
entries.alsoFixed: The R8.1.3 test asserted that this function was EXPORTED 'for ops surfaces', which pinned a second drifted implementation in place. The assertion is inverted: the gate now requires exactly one scheduled sweep of this table, and that it is the worker's.

entries.capability: the lastSeenAtUtc heartbeat behind the session inventory a user sees when reviewing their active sessions
entries.evidence: Its docblock said it was 'called by the auth middleware on permission check', and the auth middleware did not call it. What the middleware calls is recordHeartbeat in the same module, which writes the SAME column (plus lastHeartbeatAtUtc), is self-throttled to one write per session per sample window, and sits behind the SESSION_HEARTBEAT_ENABLED kill switch. So authenticated_sessions.lastSeenAtUtc is not an unwritten field — it has a live writer, and this was an unthrottled second one. That is the more dangerous half of the pair: wired as its docblock described, it would have written a hot row on EVERY authenticated request.

entries.capability: claimed to be the lastSeenAtUtc heartbeat for a contributor intake session
entries.evidence: Its docblock claimed it was 'Called from the intake-session middleware on every successful contributor request'. No intake-session middleware called it. The question that decides the disposition was then asked rather than assumed: does anything DISPLAY or DECIDE on workflow_intake_sessions.last_seen_at_utc? It does not. Neither projection over that table exposes it — loadSessionAggregateByLink selects status and the five lifecycle timestamps, loadIntakeLinkSubmissions maps to a payload with no such field — no report or verification package reads it, and the reviewer/contributor session-timeout policy is evaluated against AuthenticatedSession, not this table. Wiring it would have added a per-request write on an external-contributor hot path to feed a column with no reader.
entries.residualNote: The column itself is left in place: dropping it would need a migration to reclaim storage nothing is spending.

entries.capability: the lastSeenAtUtc heartbeat for a team membership, which the members roster displays
entries.evidence: TeamMember.lastSeenAtUtc is not decorative. The workspace administration console renders it as a 'Last seen' column in MembersSection, fed by GET /v1/identity/members through listTeamMembersWithAccess, which selects the column. Nothing wrote it, so the column was blank for every member of every workspace and an administrator deciding whether an account is dormant could not tell 'never seen' from 'never recorded'.
entries.integration: The authenticated-request path, chained off the existing session heartbeat. Reaching that line means the token verified, the session was not revoked, the security policy allowed the request and the session-timeout policy did not expire it — a FAILED authentication returns long before, so a rejected request can never advance a member's last-seen. The tenant is the session row's own anchor, not a caller-supplied header.
entries.alsoFixed: Throttled twice over. The caller only proceeds when the session heartbeat itself decided to write, inheriting its sample window; and the write's own WHERE requires lastSeenAtUtc to be null or older than the window, so two concurrent requests inside one window produce at most one write regardless of what either caller believed. Suspended and revoked memberships are excluded — a revoked row must not look like it was used after revocation.
